title: Nikiforov–Rousseau Question on Best p-Goodness Threshold for Books
statement_text: What is the best possible $n$ (in terms of $k$ and $p$) such that $B_{k,n}$ is $p$-good, i.e., such that $r(K_p, B_{k,n}) = (p-1)(n-1)+1$?
context_text: Nikiforov and Rousseau proved via Szemerédi's regularity lemma that for every $k, p \geq 2$ and every sufficiently large $n$, the book $B_{k,n}$ is $p$-good, but their proof yields only a tower-type bound on $n$. They raised the question of determining the best possible $n$. The present paper addresses this by providing a regularity-free proof with a single-exponential bound.
paper_contribution: Provides a new proof avoiding the regularity lemma, establishing that $B_{k,n}$ is $p$-good for all $n \geq 2^{k^{10p}}$, replacing the tower-type bound with a single exponential; the authors note the bound is not expected to be best possible.
notes: PDF source — exponent in bound reconstructed as $k^{10p}$ from proof context ($z^z = 2^{2z\log z} \leq 2^{k^{10p}}$); question attributed to Nikiforov–Rousseau in prose without a labelled environment.

title: Informal Belief on Non-Optimality of p-Goodness Bound
statement_text: The bound $n \geq 2^{k^{10p}}$, which the authors prove sufficient for the $k$-book $B_{k,n}$ to be $p$-good (i.e. $r(K_p,B_{k,n})=(p-1)(n-1)+1$ for all $k,p\ge2$ and $n\ge 2^{k^{10p}}$), is not best possible.
context_text: The Ramsey number $r(G,H)$ is the least $N$ such that every $N$-vertex graph contains $G$ or its complement contains $H$. Burr showed $r(G,H)\ge(\chi(G)-1)(|V(H)|-1)+s(G)$ for connected $H$ with at least $s(G)$ vertices, where $s(G)$ is the minimum size of a colour class in a proper $\chi(G)$-colouring of $G$; $H$ is $G$-good if equality holds, and $p$-good if moreover $G=K_p$, i.e. $r(K_p,H)=(p-1)(|V(H)|-1)+1$. For $n\ge k\ge1$, the $k$-book $B_{k,n}$ is the $n$-vertex graph consisting of a clique $K_k$ (the spine) and $n-k$ further vertices, pairwise non-adjacent, each adjacent to all of the spine. Nikiforov and Rousseau proved, using Szemerédi's regularity lemma, that $B_{k,n}$ is $p$-good for $n$ sufficiently large, with a tower-type bound, and asked for the best possible $n$. The authors give a regularity-free proof with the bound $n\ge2^{k^{10p}}$ and say they do not expect it to be best possible. In their concluding remarks they ask for the Ramsey goodness threshold, i.e. the smallest $n$ with $r(K_p,B_{k,n})=(p-1)(n-1)+1$: a random construction shows it is at least $(k/\log p)^{cp}$ for an absolute constant $c>0$, and it would be interesting to determine whether, for fixed $p$, the correct behaviour is polynomial or exponential in $k$. Improving the bound to one single-exponential in both $k$ and $p$ would give progress on a conjecture of Conlon, Fox and Sudakov on empty pairs in triangle-free graphs.
notes: PDF source — exponent reconstructed as $k^{10p}$ from surrounding proof; stated in prose as 'We do not expect the bound $n \geq 2k^{10p}$ to be best possible'.

title: Question on Eliminating the Regularity Lemma from Nikiforov–Rousseau's General Theorem
statement_text: Is it possible to completely eliminate the use of the regularity lemma from the proof of the general Ramsey goodness theorem of Nikiforov and Rousseau (Theorem 2.1 of their paper 'Ramsey goodness and beyond', Combinatorica 2009)?
context_text: The Ramsey number $r(G,H)$ is the least $N$ such that every $N$-vertex graph contains $G$ or its complement contains $H$. Burr showed $r(G,H)\ge(\chi(G)-1)(|V(H)|-1)+s(G)$ for connected $H$ with at least $s(G)$ vertices, where $s(G)$ is the minimum size of a colour class in a proper $\chi(G)$-colouring of $G$; $H$ is $G$-good if equality holds, and $p$-good if moreover $G=K_p$, i.e. $r(K_p,H)=(p-1)(|V(H)|-1)+1$. For $n\ge k\ge1$, the $k$-book $B_{k,n}$ is the $n$-vertex graph consisting of a clique $K_k$ (the spine) and $n-k$ further vertices, pairwise non-adjacent, each adjacent to all of the spine. Using Szemerédi's regularity lemma (hence with tower-type quantitative bounds), Nikiforov and Rousseau proved a very general goodness theorem, the most general result in the field, giving tight bounds on $r(G,H)$ for several families of sparse graphs $G,H$ with $|V(G)|<\delta|V(H)|$; it implies for instance that clique subdivisions and large planar graphs are $p$-good, and that $r(B_{p-1,\delta n},B_{k,n})=(p-1)(n-1)+1$ for large $n$. The authors avoid the regularity lemma for special cases: $B_{k,n}$ is $p$-good for $n\ge2^{k^{10p}}$, and for a complete $p$-partite graph $G$ with parts $a_1\le\dots\le a_{p-1}\le t$ and $a_p\le\delta n$, $r(G,B_{k,n})=(p-1)(n-1)+a_1$ if and only if $a_1=a_2=1$, with double-exponential bounds on $1/\delta$. They ask how far these ideas can be pushed, since a regularity-free proof of the general theorem would likely give much better quantitative bounds.
notes: Posed in prose in the introduction as 'for example, is it possible to completely eliminate the use of the regularity lemma from the proof of [28, Theorem 2.1]?'.
